title: Creating and Managing Schemas
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Creating and Managing Schemas.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to create schema.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Creating and Managing Schemas. Its primary job is to help you define and evolve schemas with constraints, generated values and changes that are safe for populated tables. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing creating and managing schemas teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: define and evolve schemas with constraints, generated values and changes that are safe for populated tables. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Creating and Managing Schemas
content_blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE products (
  id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  sku text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name text NOT NULL,
  price numeric(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0),
  available boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true
);
content_blocks.expected_output: Creates a products table with an identity primary key and constraints for SKU uniqueness, required fields and nonnegative prices.
content_blocks.safety_note: Schema-changing example; use migrations and review constraints against existing records.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in a disposable database. Check the database version and inspect the resulting table definition.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Creating and Managing Schemas”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “CREATE SCHEMA”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “CREATE SCHEMA”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Creating and Managing Schemas, with an explanation of “CREATE SCHEMA”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Creating and Managing Schemas fits into the broader goal to define and evolve schemas with constraints, generated values and changes that are safe for populated tables.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: CREATE SCHEMA, Organizing objects into schemas, Schema ownership.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
